phase3_findings.description: On MySQL, a schema-qualified call to a stored function whose name is a digit followed by 'e' (for example db.1e()) is not checked: sqlglot's MySQL tokenizer reads 1e as a NUMBER token, so _called_names skips it, and the RLS re-render keeps db.1e() unchanged (confirmed by running sqlglot 30.26.0; MySQL execution not run). The unqualified 1e(id) re-renders as '1e AS (id)'.

The require_base_tables flag now asks runners to refuse views, PostgreSQL child tables, calls to database-defined routines and failed lookups, but its name still says only 'base tables'; the wider contract lives only in docstrings and RlsGuardRunner.__init__ checks only that the parameter is declared.

_refuse_database_routines sends every non-postgres dialect down the MySQL information_schema.ROUTINES branch, relying on the caller's dialect check to keep SQLite out, while _verify_relations raises RlsError for an unknown dialect; the two helpers treat an unexpected dialect differently.
_verify_relations reads the PostgreSQL child flag positionally as row[3]; a SELECT-list reorder that puts another boolean at index 3 would pass the isinstance check unnoticed.

assert_no_denied_functions, a new public sqlglot entry point on untrusted SQL, has no direct test; its 'stmt is None' branch and its walk over more than one statement are never exercised because apply_rls rejects such input first.

test_untokenizable_or_unparsable_sql_fails_closed never reaches the tokenizer failure path in _called_names on its own, because verify_base_tables calls _relations (sqlglot.parse) first and it raises first; the path still fails closed through the broad except.

The new connector tests' finally blocks run two unguarded DROP statements; if the first raises, it replaces the test's own failure and the second table is left behind (also lines 260-262; same pattern as the existing view test).

## Verdict: APPROVE with notes (7 Suggestion findings and 5 inconclusive checklist items; nothing at the Critical threshold)

The PR is ready to merge: no reviewer finding and no checklist item reaches the Critical threshold, and the only checklist FAIL at that level was overturned on re-verification.

Rule applied: rule 6 — findings below the threshold and inconclusive checklist items remain → APPROVE with notes

## Code Review Findings

### 🟡 Suggestion / Minor (7)

<details><summary>7 items</summary>

1. `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` (lines 98-106, `_called_names`): on MySQL, a schema-qualified call to a stored function whose name is a digit followed by `e` (for example `db.1e()`) is not checked. sqlglot's MySQL tokenizer reads `1e` as a NUMBER token, so `_called_names` skips it, and the RLS re-render keeps `db.1e()` unchanged. Running sqlglot 30.26.0 confirmed the token shape and the re-render. Whether MySQL then calls a stored function named `1e` was not run against a server. The unqualified form `1e(id)` is re-rendered as `1e AS (id)`, so it calls nothing. The checklist item on this tokenizer property (item VC-29) is inconclusive for the same reason. (raised by 1/6 agents; completeness critic)
2. `src/sqllens/agent/capabilities/sql_runner/base.py` (lines 23-33): the `require_base_tables` flag now asks a runner to refuse views, PostgreSQL child tables, calls to database-defined routines and failed lookups. Its name still says only "base tables". The wider contract exists only in docstrings, and `RlsGuardRunner.__init__` checks only that the parameter is declared, so a custom runner could implement the view check alone without anything noticing. (raised by 1/6 agents)
3. `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` (lines 238-270, `_refuse_database_routines`): every dialect other than `postgres` takes the MySQL `information_schema.ROUTINES` branch. That SQLite runs no routine lookup depends on the caller's `dialect in ("postgres", "mysql")` check (line 125), not on this function. `_verify_relations` instead raises `RlsError` for an unknown dialect, so the two helpers treat an unexpected dialect differently. Behavior is correct for the three dialects that reach this code today. (raised by 1/6 agents)
4. `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` (lines 182-201): `_verify_relations` reads the child flag as `row[3]` from an untyped cursor row. A short row or a non-boolean value fails closed, but reordering the SELECT list so that another boolean column lands at index 3 would pass the `isinstance` check unnoticed. (raised by 1/6 agents)
5. `src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py` (lines 565-579): `assert_no_denied_functions` is a new public sqlglot entry point on untrusted SQL, but it has no direct test. Its `stmt is None` branch ("empty parse tree") and its loop over more than one statement are never exercised. Its only tests go through `RlsGuardRunner`, where `apply_rls` already rejects such input first. (raised by 1/6 agents)
6. `tests/unit/test_rls_views.py` (lines 653-659): `test_untokenizable_or_unparsable_sql_fails_closed` never reaches the tokenizer failure path in `_called_names` on its own. `verify_base_tables` calls `_relations` (which runs `sqlglot.parse`) first, so `_relations` raises first in both cases. The failure path is still covered by the broad `except Exception`, so it fails closed. (raised by 1/6 agents)
7. `tests/connectors/test_connectors.py` (lines 228-230 and 260-262): each new connector test's `finally` block runs two `DROP` statements with no guard. When the first drop raises, that exception replaces the test's own failure and the second table is left behind. The existing view test uses the same pattern. (raised by 1/6 agents)

</details>

### ℹ️ Informational — Deferred (5)

<details><summary>5 items</summary>

- VC-26: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — The external doc and changelog name pg_sleep and generate_series as functions on the read-only guard's blocklist for PostgreSQL. [docs/external/row-level-security.md:134]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  FAIL stored INCONCLUSIVE (requirement quote is missing): Code: readonly.py:354 lists pg_sleep in the postgres set, and _DENIED_BY_DIALECT (readonly.py:423-426) unions _ALWAYS_DENIED_FUNCS (generate_series, :416-418) into every dialect, so both are on the PostgreSQL blocklist. The doc (docs/external/row-level-security.md:134) names both. The changelog entry the PR adds (diff.patch:32-34) names only `pg_sleep` ('for example `pg_sleep`'); generate_series appears nowhere in the changelog text. The claim says the doc AND changelog name both, so it is wrong for the changelog. Low impact since the changelog gives only an example. The rejection line covers a different subject (MySQL routine lookup test).

  </details>

- VC-28: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — _called_names obtains a dialect instance with sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise(dialect), reads type(instance).tokenizer_class.KEYWORDS and calls instance.tokenize(sql). These attributes and methods exist with these shapes across the pinned sqlglot range (>=25.0,<31). [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:94]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  relations.py:94-96 calls sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise(dialect), type(instance).tokenizer_class.KEYWORDS and instance.tokenize(sql); pyproject.toml:44 pins sqlglot>=25.0,<31. Read the installed sqlglot 30.26.0 (high end): dialect.py has classmethod get_or_raise (l.1047), class attr tokenizer_class = Tokenizer set per dialect by the metaclass (l.316, 903), tokenize(self, sql) -> list[Token] (l.1286), and tokens.py declares Tokenizer.KEYWORDS (l.229). A 30.2.x copy under implement-304/.prflow/tmp also shows tokenizer_class (l.291, 840). No sqlglot 25.x-29.x copy exists in the local environment (searched for sqlglot-2[5-9]* and dist-info), so the low end of the range (25.0) was not read; the claim spans the whole range, so the verdict cannot rest on the high end alone. Missing evidence: sqlglot 25.0 dialect.py/tokens.py (or running pip install sqlglot==25.0.0 and inspecting these attributes).

  </details>

- VC-29: INCONCLUSIVE (important) — Every name written immediately before '(' in call position (bare, schema-qualified, quoted or backtick-quoted) produces a token whose token_type is VAR or IDENTIFIER, or whose upper-cased text is a key of the dialect tokenizer's KEYWORDS. A call name tokenized as some other type and absent from KEYWORDS would not be collected or looked up. [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:98]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Traced sqlglot tokenizer_core.py (_scan_keywords 826-885, _scan_var 1145-1161, _scan_number 959-1038). Multi-word/keyword matches add text=word.upper() that is in KEYWORDS; _scan_var yields VAR or keywords.get(text.upper()); quoted names are IDENTIFIER. So for ordinary names (bare, qualified, quoted, backticked) the claim holds. Counterexample to the literal claim: MySQL name like `1e(`. _scan_number consumes '1', then 'e' as a scientific marker (scientific=1), then peek '(' hits the else/break; it emits NUMBER '1e' (line 1034), not VAR (the identifiers_can_start_with_digit VAR path at 1020-1021 is only reached when an identifier char follows). Token type NUMBER and '1E' not in KEYWORDS, so relations.py:101-103 would skip it. MySQL itself lexes '1e' without exponent digits as an identifier, so a stored function so named could be called unnoticed. However, no unchanged requirement text in both views demands this property (base docs/internal/database-connectors/row-level-security.md:45 says stored functions were an uninspected gap; the call check is added by the PR), so no FAIL requirement can be quoted; the claim is not shown correct either, so INCONCLUSIVE. I did not execute the tokenizer (no shell available); the trace is by reading.

  </details>

- VC-52: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — Under a rule on orders with read_only off, RlsGuardRunner passes 'WITH d AS (DELETE FROM public_values RETURNING id) SELECT id FROM d' to the inner runner byte-for-byte unchanged, and with no rules passes 'SELECT pg_sleep(1)' unchanged. [tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:787]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Second half confirmed: apply_rls returns `sql` unchanged when `not rules` (rls.py:219-220), and RlsGuardRunner skips the denylist when rules is empty (safety/__init__.py:196-197), so 'SELECT pg_sleep(1)' reaches the inner runner as-is (test at tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:797-801). First half not settled by reading: with a rule on orders, apply_rls does not short-circuit for unreferenced tables. It parses, runs traverse_scope, and returns tree.sql(dialect=dialect) (rls.py:332), a sqlglot re-render. The inner runner therefore receives the original text only if sqlglot's postgres generator happens to reproduce 'WITH d AS (DELETE FROM public_values RETURNING id) SELECT id FROM d' exactly. Nothing in the code guarantees that. I also cannot confirm that traverse_scope accepts a DELETE CTE without raising. I had no way to execute sqlglot or the test (command not run: pytest tests/unit/test_rls_views.py::test_denylist_check_adds_no_select_only_checks). The rejection line concerns the MySQL routine lookup and does not cover this claim.

  </details>

- VC-54: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — The test comment states the rewrite emits STRPOS on sqlglot 25.x and POSITION on 30.x. [tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:624]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  The 30.x half is confirmed: installed sqlglot 30.26.0 generators/postgres.py:416 has `exp.StrPosition: lambda self, e: strposition_sql(self, e, func_name="POSITION")`. The 25.x half (STRPOS) could not be verified: pyproject.toml:44 pins sqlglot>=25.0,<31, but no sqlglot 25.x source exists in any searched environment (found only 30.26.0, 30.27.0 and two 3.0.x copies), and I did not run a 25.x install. The test (tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:624-628) only asserts membership in {position, strpos}, so it does not settle which name 25.x emits. Missing evidence: sqlglot 25.x dialects/postgres.py StrPosition handling or a run of apply_rls on 25.x.

  </details>

</details>

acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured on PostgreSQL, a statement that references a relation recorded as a child in `pg_inherits` is refused with `RlsError` before it executes. This covers a declarative partition (`PARTITION OF`) and a traditional inheritance child (`INHERITS`), at any depth and in any position (top-level `FROM`, join, subquery, CTE body), whether or not a rule names the child or its parent. A rule naming a child table no longer makes that child queryable. A query on the hierarchy's top-level table still runs and returns only rows that match that table's rules, including rows stored in its children.
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured on PostgreSQL or MySQL, and with `database.read_only` true or false, a statement is refused with `RlsError` before it executes when it uses call syntax (`name(...)`, schema-qualified or not) with a name that matches, ignoring case, the name of a routine defined in the database. On PostgreSQL that means any `pg_proc` entry outside the `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` schemas, extension-installed routines included. On MySQL it means any stored function listed in `information_schema.ROUTINES`. Matching uses the routine name alone, across every schema and every argument signature. It covers such calls in the select list, `FROM`, joins, filters, aggregates and window functions, including statements that reference no relation. The names checked are the names called in the SQL that will execute after the RLS rewrite, including calls sqlglot parses as recognized built-in function nodes.
- [ ] While RLS rules are active, the read-only guard's function blocklist applies even when `database.read_only` is false: a statement that calls a function on that blocklist is refused before it executes with `UnsafeSqlError`, which reaches the MCP client as the read-only guard's refusals do today. Only the blocklist check is added on that path; with `database.read_only` false, the statement-type checks (SELECT-only) do not start applying. With no RLS rules configured, behavior for either value of `database.read_only` is unchanged. Unit tests cover, with `database.read_only` false: a blocklisted call under a rule refused; a statement that the RLS rewrite accepts but the SELECT-only checks would refuse (for example a PostgreSQL data-modifying CTE on a table without a rule) not refused by the new check; and a blocklisted call with no rules configured not refused, as today.
- [ ] Functions on the read-only guard's function blocklist are blocked while rules are active, whatever `database.read_only` is: with `database.read_only` true by the existing read-only guard, and with it false by the previous criterion. This change leaves the blocklist's entries as they are; the blocklist additions are delivered in a separate change.
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured, the routine check and the blocklist check do not refuse a statement whose called names are all outside the read-only guard's function blocklist and match no routine name that the database-defined routine check looks up, and such a statement that the other RLS checks accept keeps running with its rule predicates applied. Tests cover at minimum `count(*)` and `upper()` on PostgreSQL and MySQL, plus a PostgreSQL call that sqlglot parses as a typed node with a different canonical name (`strpos`).
- [ ] When a child or routine catalog lookup raises any exception, or the child lookup returns a child flag that is not a boolean, the query is refused with an `RlsError` whose message carries no driver detail. The cause is logged with a traceback, as for the existing relation lookup. A SQL text the check's sqlglot step cannot parse or tokenize is also refused with `RlsError`. The refusal is the same exception type through the same wrappers as the existing view refusal, so it reaches the MCP client exactly as a view refusal does, never as rows.
- [ ] Apart from the blocklist criterion, SQLite RLS behavior is unchanged: SQLite runs no child or routine lookup, and its existing RLS tests pass unmodified.
- [ ] Unit tests in `tests/unit/test_rls_views.py` drive `verify_base_tables` and the PostgreSQL and MySQL runners with fake cursors. They cover at minimum: child refused; a parent that is not a child allowed; a function call with no relation reference refused; a matching name in another schema or another letter case refused; a call whose name the sqlglot tokenizer reads as a keyword (for example `replace`), with a matching routine, refused; a built-in-only call allowed; and a raising lookup and a non-boolean child flag, both refused without echoing the driver detail. A routine lookup that returns no row allows the call.
- [ ] Connector tests in `tests/connectors/test_connectors.py` against real PostgreSQL create two protected parents: a partitioned table with a `PARTITION OF` child, and an ordinary table with an `INHERITS` child. They assert that each child query is blocked and that each parent query returns only scoped rows. They also create a SQL function that reads the protected table, and assert that calling it is blocked unqualified and schema-qualified. Against real MySQL, they create a stored function that reads the protected table and assert that both the unqualified and the schema-qualified call are blocked. On both engines, a built-in-only query on the protected table still returns scoped rows.
- [ ] In `docs/external/row-level-security.md#limitations`, the bullet opening "Rules match table names, not every path to the same rows" is replaced, and no Limitations bullet tells operators to add a rule per child table. The new bullet states that partition and inheritance child tables are unavailable while RLS is active and that rules belong on the top-level table. A second statement says that on PostgreSQL, calls to functions outside the `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` schemas, extension functions included, and on MySQL, calls to stored functions, are blocked while RLS is active, and that a built-in call is also blocked when such a function shares its name. The bullet keeps a least-privilege instruction to grant the SQL Lens database user `EXECUTE` only on routines the operator has reviewed. It does not claim that SQL Lens inspects every way the database can run stored code.
- [ ] In `docs/internal/database-connectors/row-level-security.md`, the "Database relation checks" section describes the child check (`pg_inherits`) and the routine check (`pg_proc` outside `pg_catalog`/`information_schema`; MySQL `information_schema.ROUTINES`; case-insensitive name match; runs with no relation references), and their fail-closed lookups. The paragraph opening "Known gaps with the same root cause" no longer describes these two paths as open. "Unprotected base-table queries still work" names the child-table exception. The custom-runner paragraph states that runners beneath `RlsGuardRunner` must enforce these checks too. The sentences in `docs/internal/database-connectors/read-only-safety.md` and in this page that say `database.read_only = false` skips the parser guard state that the function blocklist still applies while RLS rules are configured.
- [ ] A `changelog.d/<PR>.security.md` fragment states the outcome and the operator action: query top-level tables and move child rules to the parent, and note that, under RLS, calls to PostgreSQL functions outside `pg_catalog`/`information_schema` and to MySQL stored functions are blocked, and that while rules are active the read-only guard's function blocklist applies even when `database.read_only` is false. `changelog.d/274.security.md` is unchanged.

Read the installed sqlglot 30.26.0 (high end): dialect.py has classmethod get_or_raise (l.1047), class attr tokenizer_class = Tokenizer set per dialect by the metaclass (l.316, 903), tokenize(self, sql) -> list[Token] (l.1286), and tokens.py declares Tokenizer.KEYWORDS (l.229). A 30.2.x copy under implement-304/.prflow/tmp also shows tokenizer_class (l.291, 840). No sqlglot 25.x-29.x copy exists in the local environment (searched for sqlglot-2[5-9]* and dist-info), so the low end of the range (25.0) was not read; the claim spans the whole range, so the verdict cannot rest on the high end alone. Missing evidence: sqlglot 25.0 dialect.py/tokens.py (or running pip install sqlglot==25.0.0 and inspecting these attributes).

checklist.claim: Every name written immediately before '(' in call position (bare, schema-qualified, quoted or backtick-quoted) produces a token whose token_type is VAR or IDENTIFIER, or whose upper-cased text is a key of the dialect tokenizer's KEYWORDS. A call name tokenized as some other type and absent from KEYWORDS would not be collected or looked up.
checklist.verify_against: sqlglot tokenizer (sqlglot/tokens.py) and the postgres and mysql dialect tokenizers
checklist.verify_hint: Check Tokenizer._scan_var / _scan_keywords in sqlglot/tokens.py and the KEYWORDS of the Postgres and MySQL Tokenizer subclasses for token types (e.g. single-token types, multi-word keyword keys) a function name can take that are neither VAR/IDENTIFIER nor a KEYWORDS key matching token.text.upper()
checklist.evidence: Traced sqlglot tokenizer_core.py (_scan_keywords 826-885, _scan_var 1145-1161, _scan_number 959-1038). Multi-word/keyword matches add text=word.upper() that is in KEYWORDS; _scan_var yields VAR or keywords.get(text.upper()); quoted names are IDENTIFIER. So for ordinary names (bare, qualified, quoted, backticked) the claim holds. Counterexample to the literal claim: MySQL name like `1e(`. _scan_number consumes '1', then 'e' as a scientific marker (scientific=1), then peek '(' hits the else/break; it emits NUMBER '1e' (line 1034), not VAR (the identifiers_can_start_with_digit VAR path at 1020-1021 is only reached when an identifier char follows). Token type NUMBER and '1E' not in KEYWORDS, so relations.py:101-103 would skip it. MySQL itself lexes '1e' without exponent digits as an identifier, so a stored function so named could be called unnoticed. However, no unchanged requirement text in both views demands this property (base docs/internal/database-connectors/row-level-security.md:45 says stored functions were an uninspected gap; the call check is added by the PR), so no FAIL requirement can be quoted; the claim is not shown correct either, so INCONCLUSIVE. I did not execute the tokenizer (no shell available); the trace is by reading.

checklist.evidence: Second half confirmed: apply_rls returns `sql` unchanged when `not rules` (rls.py:219-220), and RlsGuardRunner skips the denylist when rules is empty (safety/__init__.py:196-197), so 'SELECT pg_sleep(1)' reaches the inner runner as-is (test at tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:797-801). It parses, runs traverse_scope, and returns tree.sql(dialect=dialect) (rls.py:332), a sqlglot re-render. The inner runner therefore receives the original text only if sqlglot's postgres generator happens to reproduce 'WITH d AS (DELETE FROM public_values RETURNING id) SELECT id FROM d' exactly. Nothing in the code guarantees that. I also cannot confirm that traverse_scope accepts a DELETE CTE without raising. I had no way to execute sqlglot or the test (command not run: pytest tests/unit/test_rls_views.py::test_denylist_check_adds_no_select_only_checks). The rejection line concerns the MySQL routine lookup and does not cover this claim.
